title: The port
prompt: Ana and Ben port a 10-module codebase to the new framework. They split it in half: Ana starts from the top, Ben from the bottom. Ana ports 1 module an hour, Ben ports 2. When both halves are done, what percent of the modules did Ana port?
hint: Read the second sentence again. Who decided how much each person does?
explain: 50. They split it in half before starting, so speed never mattered. Ben just finished first and went for coffee.

title: The sinking cluster
prompt: The old cluster dies in exactly 20 minutes. 15 services are still on it. The migration job moves 5 at a time, but one slot must always carry the coordinator, who rides back for the next batch. A one-way trip takes 4 minutes. How many services can you save?
hint: Count trips: over, back, over, back, over. The last trip does not need to come back.
explain: 13. Trips leave at minute 0, 8 and 16, each carrying 4 services plus the coordinator. The last trip at minute 16 can fill all 5 slots. 4 + 4 + 5 = 13.

title: Left running
prompt: Ten laptops sit on the office table on battery, all running the test suite. Before you leave you close two of them. Later, someone closes one more. The rest run all night. In the morning, how many laptops still have battery?
hint: Think about what a laptop running on battery all night looks like by morning.
explain: 3. The seven that kept running are dead. Only the three that were closed still have charge. Sometimes the answer is the boring one.

title: The doubling log
prompt: A bug makes one log line copy itself every minute: 1 line, then 2, then 4, and so on. After 60 minutes the disk is full. After how many minutes was the disk half full?
hint: Each minute the size doubles. Work backwards from full.
explain: 59. If it doubles every minute, half full is one minute before full. The disk was fine for almost an hour and then it was not.

title: Two branches
prompt: Two engineers compare branches. 'If I moved 2 commits from my branch to yours, yours would have twice as many as mine.' 'And if you moved one more on top of that, mine would have three times yours.' How many commits does each branch have right now?
hint: Both branches have the same number. Try small numbers: 5, 6, 7.
explain: 6 each. Move two: 4 and 8, twice. Move one more: 3 and 9, three times. Both branches are identical; both engineers are stubborn.

title: Half of itself
prompt: A reviewer asks how long the router contract is. 'As many lines as your pull request, plus half of its own length.' Your pull request is 22 lines. How many lines is the contract?
hint: Half of the contract is 22 lines, then.
explain: 44. If the contract is your 22 lines plus half of itself, your 22 lines are the other half. So the whole thing is 44.

title: The receipt
prompt: The company laptop and its charger cost $1,100 together. The laptop costs $1,000 more than the charger. How much does the charger cost?
hint: It is not $100. Check: does laptop minus charger equal $1,000?
explain: $50. Charger 50, laptop 1,050: together 1,100 and the gap is exactly 1,000. Almost everyone says 100 first.

title: Three laptops
prompt: Three engineers leave identical laptops in the locker overnight. In the morning each grabs one without looking at the sticker. What is the chance that exactly two of them get their own laptop?
hint: If two people have their own, whose laptop is left for the third?
explain: Zero. If two people hold their own laptops, the only one left is the third person's own. Exactly two is impossible.

title: Servers and jobs
prompt: 5 servers process 5 jobs in 5 minutes. How many servers do you need to process 100 jobs in 100 minutes?
hint: How many jobs does one server finish in 5 minutes? And in 100 minutes?
explain: 5. One server does one job in 5 minutes, so 20 jobs in 100 minutes. Five servers do 100. The numbers were dressed up to look scary.

title: Launch day
prompt: Sara says: 'The day after tomorrow the protocol turns 2 years old. But on New Year's Day last year it had not launched yet, and it launched 1 year before that anniversary.' Wait, simpler: 'The day after tomorrow I turn 30, but on New Year's Day last year I was still 27.' What is today's date?
hint: If she is 27 on New Year's Day last year and 30 the day after tomorrow, three birthdays fit in barely two years. Only one date makes that work.
explain: December 31. Her birthday is January 2. Last New Year's Day she was 27; she turned 28 on January 2 last year, 29 this January, and turns 30 the day after tomorrow.

title: Splitting the monorepo
prompt: A monorepo holds 30 packages in one block. Each split step takes one block and breaks it into two. How many split steps until all 30 packages stand alone?
hint: Every split increases the number of blocks by exactly one. Start at 1 block, end at 30.
explain: 29. Each step adds one block. From 1 to 30 is 29 steps, however you choose to cut. The migration plan was never the hard part.

title: Two offers
prompt: Two teams want you. Team A pays $100,000 a year with a $20,000 raise every year. Team B pays $50,000 every half year with a $5,000 raise every half year. Purely on money, which offer pays more?
hint: Write out the first two years for both. Half-year raises come twice a year.

title: The on-call split
prompt: On the way out you handled the first 180 alerts and your colleague the rest. On the way back your colleague took the first 100 and you took the rest, same total. How many more alerts did you handle than your colleague?
hint: Call the total per leg T. You did 180 + (T minus 100). They did (T minus 180) + 100. The T cancels.
explain: 160. You: T + 80. Them: T minus 80. Difference 160, whatever T is. You should mention this in the retro.

title: The rollout
prompt: Rolling out from region 1 to region 4 took 48 minutes at a steady pace. At the same pace, how long from region 4 to region 8?
hint: Count the steps between regions, not the region numbers. 1 to 4 is three steps.
explain: 64 minutes. 1 to 4 is 3 steps, 16 minutes each. 4 to 8 is 4 steps: 64. Off-by-one, the classic.

title: The rack
prompt: 27 identical servers are stacked in a 3 by 3 by 3 cube. Only faces on the outside of the cube get a network cable. How many servers have exactly one cabled face?
hint: Where in a cube does a small cube touch the outside on exactly one side?
explain: 6, the centre of each face. Corners have 3 cabled faces, edges 2, the very middle server has none and should be worried.

title: The flaky test
prompt: A flaky test fails 1 time in 6. It has just failed on two deploys in a row. What is the chance it fails on the third?
hint: The test has no memory. What were the odds before the first deploy?
explain: 1 in 6. Each run is independent; the two failures already happened. Streaks feel meaningful to people, not to dice.

title: The last letter
prompt: The first letter of the protocol is U, and the second is N. But the letter you need to worry about is the last one. What is the last letter of the protocol?
hint: Read the question literally. Which word is 'the protocol'?
explain: L. The last letter of the word 'protocol'. Not of Uniswap, not of the alphabet. Reading the ticket carefully is half the job.

title: Who broke the build
prompt: Three teammates, and exactly one of them tells the truth. Ana: 'It was not me.' Ben: 'It was Cai.' Cai: 'Ben is lying.' Who broke the build?
hint: Try each suspect and count how many statements come out true. Only one case gives exactly one.
explain: Ana. If Ana did it: Ana lies, Ben lies, Cai tells the truth. Exactly one. Any other suspect makes two people truthful.

title: The whiteboard
prompt: Someone left cards on the whiteboard: O, T, T, F, ?, S, S, E, N. Which letter goes on the blank card?
hint: Say them out loud, as counting.
explain: F. One, Two, Three, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight, Nine. The first letters. Whoever left it also drank the last coffee.

title: The validator square
prompt: Nine validators sit in a 3 by 3 grid, staking 1 to 9 coins each, every number used once. Every row, column and diagonal stakes 15 in total. How many coins does the validator in the centre stake?
hint: The centre appears in four lines: one row, one column, both diagonals. Add the four lines and see how often each cell is counted.
explain: 5. Add the four lines through the centre: 4 times 15 = 60, which counts the centre four times and everything else once. Everything sums to 45, so 3 centres = 15. Centre is 5.

title: The light artifact
prompt: Eight build artifacts look identical, but one is missing a file and is lighter. You have a scale that compares two groups. What is the fewest weighings that are guaranteed to find the light one?
hint: Do not split 4 and 4. Leave some artifacts off the scale.
explain: 2. Weigh 3 against 3. If they balance, weigh the leftover 2. If not, take the lighter 3 and weigh 1 against 1; the leftover is the answer if they balance.

title: What are they describing
prompt: Two people who have never seen an office watch you at your desk. 'It pins a stack of paper down by punching a bent piece of metal through it.' What is it?
hint: The metal bends after it goes through.
explain: A stapler. Described from the outside every office object sounds like a weapon.

title: Down the hole
prompt: Your hardware wallet rolls into a deep, narrow hole in solid rock with a bend halfway down. No hand or stick can reach it. What gets it out?
hint: What does a small plastic object do in water?
explain: Water. Fill the hole and the wallet floats up. Then never carry it in your shirt pocket again.

title: Two reviewers
prompt: Only two engineers on the team review code, and each can only be reviewed by the other. Ana's own pull requests are spotless. Ben's own pull requests are a mess. Whose reviews do you want on your code?
hint: Who reviewed Ana's spotless pull requests?
explain: Ben's. Ana's clean PRs were reviewed by Ben; Ben's messy ones were reviewed by Ana. Judge the reviewer by the other person's code.

title: Three cron jobs
prompt: Three cron jobs run every 2, 3 and 4 minutes. They all fire right now. In how many minutes do all three fire together again?
hint: Find the smallest number that 2, 3 and 4 all divide.
explain: 12. The least common multiple of 2, 3 and 4. That is also when the pager goes off three times at once.

title: The standup circle
prompt: At standup the team stands in a circle. Ana is directly opposite Ben. Counting clockwise from Ana, Ben is the 7th person. How many people are in the circle?
hint: If Ben is opposite Ana, the same count runs the other way round too.
explain: 12. Six people between them on each side: Ana, six, Ben, six more. Twelve, and one of them is always on mute.

title: The mirrored clock
prompt: You glance at the meeting-room clock in the mirror behind you. It shows 4:20. The standup starts at 8:00. How long do you have?
hint: A mirror flips the clock face. 4:20 mirrored is not 4:20.
explain: 20 minutes. Mirrored, 4:20 is 7:40. Standup is in 20 minutes and you have not read the ticket.

title: The pool rule
prompt: A trading pool holds 10 ETH and 1,000 dollars, and it follows one rule: ETH times dollars must stay 10,000 after every trade. A trader takes 5 ETH out of the pool. How many dollars must they put in?
hint: After the trade the pool has 5 ETH. What dollar amount keeps the product at 10,000?
explain: 1,000. With 5 ETH left the pool needs 2,000 dollars to keep 5 x 2,000 = 10,000. It had 1,000, so the trader pays 1,000. Taking half the ETH doubled the price. That is Uniswap in one line.

title: Half the coins
prompt: Same rule: coins times dollars stays constant. A pool holds 20 coins and 400 dollars, so one coin is worth 20 dollars. A trader pulls out 10 coins. How many dollars per coin did they pay on average?
hint: Work out the dollars after the trade first, then divide what was paid by 10.
explain: 40. Product 8,000. With 10 coins left, dollars must be 800, so the trader paid 400 for 10 coins: 40 each, double the quoted price. Big trades on small pools hurt.

title: Pick the fee
prompt: Uniswap lets pool creators pick the fee traders pay: 1%, 0.3%, 0.05% or 0.01%. A team wants to open a pool between two coins that are both pegged to the dollar and barely move against each other. Which fee attracts traders?
hint: Would you pay a 1% fee to swap a dollar for a dollar?
explain: 0.01%. The two coins are nearly the same price, so traders only come for the cheapest fee. Volatile pairs can charge more.

title: Two days later
prompt: A vote to change the protocol passes on Friday at 15:00. The rules say every passed change waits exactly 2 days before it can run, so everyone can see it coming. When is the earliest it can run?
hint: Two days from Friday afternoon. Weekends count.
explain: Sunday 15:00. The waiting period does not know about weekends. Neither, that day, do you.

title: Standup in Bangkok
prompt: Standup is at 09:00 in New York. New York is 4 hours behind universal time, and Bangkok is 7 hours ahead of it. What time is standup in Bangkok?
hint: Go from New York to universal time first (add 4), then to Bangkok (add 7).
explain: 20:00. 09:00 in New York is 13:00 universal, which is 20:00 in Bangkok. Dinner standup.

title: The loop
prompt: A payout script runs: for i from 0 up to and including list.length, pay list[i]. The list has 5 names. What happens?
choices: The first person gets paid twice
It tries to pay a 6th person that does not exist and crashes
hint: Positions in a list of 5 are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Which position is 'length'?
explain: It crashes. Position 5 does not exist in a list of 5. The whole payout stops. The oldest bug in the book, still in the book.

title: Passes at home, fails at midnight
prompt: A test passes on your laptop but fails on the build server only around midnight universal time. What is the likely bug?
choices: The test uses 'today', and the date differs between the two machines around midnight
hint: What changes about the world at exactly midnight?
explain: A date boundary. Your laptop and the server disagree about what day it is for a few hours. Fake the clock in tests.

title: Permission bits
prompt: A contract stores permissions as switches worth 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. The switches worth 1, 4 and 8 are on. What number does the contract store?
hint: Add up the switches that are on.
explain: 13. 1 + 4 + 8. Engineers hide whole settings menus inside one number this way.

title: Falling price
prompt: In one Uniswap feature, a trade starts at a price great for the trader and gets slightly worse every second until someone agrees to fill it. What kind of auction is that?
hint: Named after the flower markets that count the price down instead of up.
explain: A Dutch auction. Fillers jump in the moment it becomes worth it for them, which is exactly when the trader gets the best price anyone will give.

title: The allowance race
prompt: You gave an app permission to spend up to 100 of your coins. You now send a change lowering it to 50. The app sees your change coming and acts before it lands. What is the worst case?
hint: What can it do before your change lands, and what after?
explain: 150. It spends the old 100 first, then the new 50 arrives and it spends that too. The fix: lower to zero first, then set the new amount.
